sections.heading: Why we are writing to you

sentences.text: We are writing because public records show that GRIN1-related neurodevelopmental disorder and SLC13A5-related epileptic encephalopathy are both linked to a loss-of-function disease mechanism, although for GRIN1 there are also published claims of gain-of-function in some cases.

Public records also show high phenotype similarity between the two conditions, with overlap in reduced or abnormal eye contact, abnormal nonverbal communication, epileptic encephalopathy, and encephalopathy.
We hope to learn from a community that has natural history studies and a targeted clinical trial already in public records.
Gene2Phenotype lists a definitive gene-disease link for both GRIN1 and SLC13A5.
Gene2Phenotype also records loss of function as the curated mechanism for both conditions, and for both this is inferred rather than established by direct functional evidence in the summary record.
Published model work has been reported for both genes.
Public records show active NIH-funded research in both conditions in FY2025-2026.
Public records show that neither condition has an approved disease-specific therapy.

sections.heading: What we would like to learn from or reuse

sentences.text: Public records show two SLC13A5 natural history studies, one United States only and one remote only, and they suggest that registry design and natural history protocol may be reusable for us with review by experts.
Public records also suggest that outcome measures and endpoints may carry over, but age of onset and severity need review before anything is adopted.

The SLC13A5 community also appears to have a broader clinical network through its natural history studies, Citizen Health, and interventional studies, and public records suggest those sites and investigators may help point us to experienced centers.

A ClinicalTrials.gov record states that SLC13A5 has a recruiting phase 1/phase 2 intrathecal gene therapy study, and public records suggest its trial design may be a useful template for expert review in GRIN1.
Public records show a patient organization for GRIN1, CureGRIN Foundation, but we found no public record of a named SLC13A5 patient organization in the sources searched here.
For GRIN1, public records show inclusion in the shared Simons Searchlight registry, but we found no public record here of a GRIN1-specific registry or natural history study.
For SLC13A5, public records show two natural history studies and inclusion in Citizen Health.
For GRIN1, public records show two pathway-level trials such as diet or supplement approaches, but no trial acting on the gene or its product was found.
For SLC13A5, a ClinicalTrials.gov record states that there is a gene-level targeted trial and another targeted interventional study that is no longer available.

We must not assume that therapeutic strategy transfers directly between our communities, because GRIN1 has published reports pointing in more than one mechanistic direction and the recorded mechanism is per gene and disease, not per family.
Our own variant would need confirmation by a clinical geneticist before any therapy logic is borrowed from SLC13A5.
We also must not assume that SLC13A5 disease models can stand in for GRIN1 models, because the model is gene-specific, even if some assay ideas may still be reusable after expert review.
We must not assume that a person with GRIN1 would be eligible for an SLC13A5 study, because public records do not assert cross-enrollment and say families should ask the study team directly.
Do the age of onset and typical severity in SLC13A5-related disease match GRIN1 closely enough for registry items, visit schedules, and outcome measures to apply well to our families.
Which mechanism class does a given GRIN1 family's variant belong to: loss of function, gain of function, or dominant negative.
Has that specific GRIN1 variant been functionally tested, and does it match the mechanism recorded for the condition.
What functional evidence exists for GRIN1, given that the curated mechanism is inferred from variant types in the summary record.
Thank you for reading.

glossary.meaning: A change that reduces how much a gene or its protein can do.
A change that makes a gene or its protein do more, or act in a new way.
A study that follows people over time to learn how a condition changes.
A way to track a person's health or function in a study.
A study aimed at the gene or its direct product rather than only symptoms or a broader pathway.
A doctor with specialist training in genetic conditions and variant interpretation.
